content: Astragalus is a large genus comprising approximately 2,000 species of herbs and small shrubs. These plants belong to the legume family Fabaceae, specifically the subfamily Faboideae. The genus is native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Common names for Astragalus species include milk-vetch (used for most species) and goat's-thorn (referring to species such as A. gummifer and A. tragacantha). While some pale-flowered vetches may resemble Astragalus species in appearance, vetches are generally more vine-like in growth habit. Astragalus species serve as food plants for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, including various case-bearers of the genus Coleophora. Specific examples include C. astragalella (which feeds exclusively on A. glycyphyllos), C. cartilaginella (which feeds exclusively on Astragalus), C. colutella, C. euryaule (which feeds exclusively on Astragalus), C. gallipennella (which feeds exclusively on A. glycyphyllos), C. hippodromica (which feeds exclusively on A. gombo), C. onobrychiella (which feeds exclusively on Astragalus), C. polonicella (which feeds exclusively on A. arenarius), and C. vicinella. Medicinal Use Astragalus membranaceus, also known as huáng qí (黄芪, meaning yellow leader) or běi qí (北芪, meaning northern leader), is a tonic herb traditionally used in Chinese medicine. It is believed to function as a galactagogue and has been shown in recent studies to potentially enhance the human immune system. The natural gum tragacanth, which is utilized in pharmaceuticals and textiles, is derived from Astragalus tragacantha. This gum is claimed to support immune function and increase the body’s resistance to common viral infections. In Western herbal medicine, Astragalus is primarily regarded as a tonic for improving metabolism and digestion. It is often consumed as a tea made from the plant's roots. Traditionally, it has also been used to strengthen the immune system and to aid in the healing of wounds and injuries. The biotech company Geron Corporation has identified a molecule from the root of Astragalus membranaceus called TA-65, which acts as a telomerase activator. According to PRNewswire, TA Sciences holds a license from Geron to market TA-65 as a nutraceutical anti-aging product, which is currently available at their TA Sciences Center in New York City. Traditional Use of Huáng Qí (Radix Astragali) Replenishes the Qi of the Spleen and Stomach. Promotes the ascension of the Yang Qi of the Spleen and Stomach. Benefits Qi and consolidates the surface, helping to control sweating. Promotes urination and reduces swelling caused by deficiency patterns. Facilitates the discharge of pus and accelerates wound healing. Tonifies and nourishes both Qi and Blood. Used in the treatment of Wasting and Thirsting syndrome (diabetes). Huáng qí is believed to enter the Lung and Spleen meridians, with properties described as sweet and slightly warm. Contraindications: It should not be used in cases of Yin deficiency with heat or in conditions of exterior excess heat. Preparation Notes: When prepared with honey, it is said to tonify Spleen and Stomach Qi. When prepared with wine, it is believed to tonify essence, and when prepared with salt, it is thought to tonify the Kidneys. Ornamental Use Several species of Astragalus are cultivated as ornamental plants in gardens. Examples include A. alpinus (which has bluish-purple flowers), A. hypoglottis (with purple flowers), and A. lotoides.
